claim: Subjective experience (qualia) exists: there is something it is like to be a conscious being

evidence.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat? (Nagel 1974)
evidence.finding: Nagel argued that consciousness has an essentially subjective character that cannot be captured by objective, physical description

evidence.title: Qualia (SEP)
evidence.finding: The existence of qualia (subjective experiential qualities) is widely accepted, though their nature and reducibility to physical processes is debated

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Subjective experience is private and first-person — it cannot be measured by third-person instruments, making correspondence near-zero by empirical standards
scoreReasoning.coherence: Consistent with virtually all philosophical and folk-psychological frameworks; even those who deny qualia acknowledge the phenomenology
scoreReasoning.convergence: Near-universal agreement that experience exists (cogito); eliminativists are a small minority
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Understanding consciousness matters for ethics, AI, medicine (anesthesia, disorders of consciousness)

claim: Specific patterns of neural activity consistently correlate with specific conscious states

evidence.title: A framework for consciousness (Dehaene & Changeux 2011)
evidence.finding: Global workspace theory identifies specific neural signatures (P3b wave, prefrontal-parietal ignition) that correlate with conscious perception

evidence.title: Neural correlates of consciousness (Koch et al.)
evidence.finding: Decades of research have identified reliable neural correlates of consciousness using fMRI, EEG, and single-cell recording

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Neuroimaging and electrophysiology directly measure neural correlates; binocular rivalry, masking paradigms provide precise experimental control
scoreReasoning.coherence: Consistent with physicalist frameworks and neuroscience more broadly
scoreReasoning.convergence: Multiple independent labs using different methods converge on similar NCC findings; some disagreement about which theory best explains them
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: NCC research informs anesthesia monitoring, brain-computer interfaces, and disorders of consciousness diagnosis

claim: Systematic, lawful relationships exist between physical stimuli and conscious experience (psychophysics)

evidence.title: On the psychophysical law (Stevens 1957)
evidence.finding: Stevens' power law describes the relationship between stimulus magnitude and perceived intensity across sensory modalities

evidence.title: The Problem of Perception (SEP)
evidence.finding: Psychophysical research demonstrates lawful, measurable relationships between physical stimuli and perceptual experience

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Psychophysical laws are directly measurable: JNDs, detection thresholds, and magnitude estimation are well-replicated
scoreReasoning.coherence: Consistent with both neuroscience and the assumption that consciousness is lawfully related to physical processes
scoreReasoning.convergence: Psychophysical laws replicated across cultures, species, and sensory modalities for over 150 years
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Applied in display technology, audiology, pain measurement, and ergonomics

claim: Explaining why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience (the 'hard problem') remains unsolved

evidence.title: The Conscious Mind (Chalmers 1996)
evidence.finding: Chalmers distinguished the 'hard problem' (why there is experience at all) from 'easy problems' (functional/behavioral explanations of cognition)

evidence.title: Consciousness (SEP)
evidence.finding: The hard problem remains one of the deepest unsolved problems in philosophy and science; no consensus on whether it can be solved within physicalism

scoreReasoning.correspondence: The claim is about the status of a problem — the 'unsolved' status is itself observable by surveying the field
scoreReasoning.coherence: Consistent with the current state of neuroscience and philosophy; acknowledges genuine explanatory gap
scoreReasoning.convergence: Broad agreement that the hard problem is genuinely hard; disagreement about whether it is solvable in principle
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Acknowledging the hard problem guides research priorities and prevents premature claims of having solved consciousness

claim: Conscious experience exists as a real phenomenon, though its relationship to physical processes remains an open and foundational question

evidence.title: Consciousness (SEP)
evidence.finding: Consciousness is widely acknowledged as a real phenomenon requiring explanation, though no theory has achieved consensus

evidence.title: Theories of consciousness (Doerig et al. 2021)
evidence.finding: Multiple competing theories of consciousness (GWT, IIT, HOT, etc.) each explain some data but none accounts for all phenomena

scoreReasoning.correspondence: The existence of consciousness is the most certain datum; its relationship to physics is uncertain and partially measurable through NCC research
scoreReasoning.coherence: Coherently integrates the certainty of experience with the uncertainty of explanation
scoreReasoning.convergence: Near-universal agreement that consciousness exists and that the mind-body problem is unsolved
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: This honest assessment guides research, ethical considerations about AI and animals, and clinical practice
